utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Very good morning, Your Honours. Case Number IT-99-36-T, The Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Brdjanin, can you follow in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Yes, I can follow in a language I can understand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Joanna Korner, Julian Nicholls, assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good morning to you. Mr. Ackerman or Mr. Cunningham, appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. David Cunningham with John Ackerman, along with Aleksandar Vujic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good morning to you. Do you have any preliminaries yourselves for the time being? Now, we are as promised coming back to you on the position we feel ought to be taken regarding the execution or stay of execution of the part of our Rule 98 decision in virtue of which we basically stated that there is -- we basically acquitted the accused of the charge of the genocide under the third category of joint criminal enterprise. Now, you will definitely all agree with us that if you look at the Rules, there are two different approaches depending on whether the accused has been found guilty or whether the accused has been acquitted. But again, it seems that the Rules address the final situation more than anything that may happen in between. The position is as follows: That when the accused is found guilty there is, according to the Rules, it seems, a stay of execution pending the outcome of the appeal, but of course the accused remains in detention. When there is an acquittal, you have the inverse, the opposite legal situation in the sense that it seems to me that you have an immediate execution of the judgement. There is release, and what the Rules provide for is actually a remedy should there be a reversal on appeal and the accused is still on release. We think that looking at the Rules, we should keep the position, the legal position, of the accused as it emerges out of our decision. I'm prejudiced in the sense that whatever we are going to decide now will not prejudice this status of the accused in regard to the third category of joint criminal enterprise in relation to genocide. However, since there is an appeal, we thought it would be wise not to ignore this fact and to suggest to you to make representations on this issue as we go along. Your case is finished in any case. You don't have any more evidence. The Defence position may be a little bit different --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's not quite right, because there's rebuttal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm not saying that we will be calling rebuttal, but that should always be kept in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would suppose, to be on the safe side, Ms. Korner, let's play it the safe way and imagine for a moment that the charge is still on in the indictment. In other words, let's -- for the time being, you are to assume that it's still before us and that we would be pleased to hear your submissions or anything that you may have in regard. However, we are making it very clear that should we arrive to the final stage of these proceedings without a final pronouncement by the Appeals Chamber on the issue, then we are going -- we are not going to go into the matter. In other words, we will stay by what we had decided in the Rule 98 bis decision. So this is why I'm saying that what we are stating now is a practical approach to the matter without, however, letting it in any way prejudice the legal status of the accused as it emerges out of the Rule 98 decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I suggest, because there are a couple of matters I want to address to you on this. But may I suggest that perhaps we leave it, because it's not going to affect anything at this moment. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At this moment, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We can have the witness. The difficulty, to summarise it, is this: Your Honours have not acquitted of a charge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, we have said that there is incompatibility between the concept of the third category of joint criminal enterprise and genocide, because of the specific intent requirement in genocide, et cetera, and so we have basically said there is no case to answer. But, that creates, if you look at the Rules, it creates a legal relationship between the accused and the Trial Chamber. And the legal relationship is such that there is nothing in the Rules which would indicate that our decision insofar as it relates to that issue would be stayed, the execution of our decision will be stayed simply because there is an appeal pending. There's nothing in the Rules which would show that; rather, if there is a legal argument to be drawn from the Rules is that in such case, the accused would have the full advantage of that decision under the law, and it will remain like that until the matter is decided upon by the Appeals Chamber. If it so happens that the Appeals Chamber would not have dealt with and determined the matter before we come to the final decision, then we are bound by our own decision. Because otherwise, it wouldn't make sense deciding a matter and reopening it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. I understand that. And Your Honour, in one sense, as we suggested in our appeal it would have been better had it been left until the end of the case because then of course Your Honours would have been able to say that as a matter of law we find that this mode of liability does not apply. Your Honour, the difficulty as I say, what Your Honours actually did was say a mode of liability we find in law cannot apply. He's not an acquitted person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We said something more important than that, Ms. Korner. Because we are fully aware of what the parameters of the Rule 98 exercise are. However, there are overriding principles, and these overriding principles are matters -- fundamental matters of substantive law, criminal law. And one of the basic principles is if a crime isn't on the statute book, it doesn't exist, one cannot be found guilty of that crime because it simply doesn't exist. So we stated in our decision that there is no such thing as criminal responsibility under the third category of joint criminal enterprise, criminal responsibility for genocide under the third category of joint criminal enterprise. So basically we were applying there the principle that as you said Judge Schomburg loves, and me, too, that there should be no guilt, if there is no crime and no punishment if there isn't a crime. So we apply--

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think I'm just repeating myself, Your Honour. I think that's the point. There's no such thing as a crime of joint criminal enterprise. The crime is genocide or persecutions or extermination or whatever it may be. The joint criminal enterprise is a method by which he may be held liable for the commission of that crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's a method of commission, a mode of commission.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I think I understand what Your Honours are saying. So as it -- although the principle is one of importance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- I don't think there's anything else I need to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. address Your Honours on. And we understand that if at the end of the day when we come to final submissions there's no Appeals Chamber' judgement, then of course Your Honours will find in the way you already found.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are bound by our own decision because it wouldn't make sense. Yes, do you have --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the only other thing, it may well be that certainly before the end of the trial, we'll get a decision in the Krstic appeal and that may say something about the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I just want to know if I can now take as a concession on behalf of the Office of the Prosecutor that joint criminal enterprise does not in any form constitute a separate offence, because I would like that very much if they're now conceding that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's a mode of commission, Mr. Ackerman. You can take it from me that --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We've never for one moment suggested an offence. It's a mode of committing the offence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's a mode of committing. And this is not something that the Prosecution has invented or I am inventing. It's something if you read practically all the decisions of this Tribunal dealing with joint criminal enterprise starting from when it was first conceived in Tadic, you will immediately realise that it's a mode of commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour. But there has also been suggestions that it relates to the law of conspiracy, which is, in effect, a commitment offence in itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, we had spent hours discussing in Chambers the difference between joint criminal enterprise, conspiracy, and complicity for that matter. And don't forget that conspiracy, for example, the idea of conspiracy is alien to practically all the civil law jurisdictions. It's only emerging now as a result of its introduction in international conventions dealing, for example, with drugs or with transnational organised crime, and that's when some countries heard for the first time about the notion of conspiracy.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour, it's in the statute in respect of genocide. For some reason, actually, nobody has ever used it, and I think that's because of the difficulties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I want to make it absolutely clear, because we dealt with it, and I think Talic's counsel raised it and suggested that joint criminal enterprise was a separate offence. We have always maintained it's never been such. It's merely a mode of commission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And we are making it very clear that never for a moment did we understand that there was a charge, a separate charge, of a joint criminal enterprise. I mean, it's -- in fact, it's one of the modes of criminal responsibility that is being put forward in the indictment. In fact, we have to go through the whole exercise if there is no responsibility under joint criminal enterprise, then we have to see whether there is individual responsibility otherwise. So yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The other possibility that we really haven't discussed Your Honour is that the Appeals Chamber may decide not to decide that this really is an issue that is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So we may not get a decision from them other than not to decide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I mean -- and I am not in a position to go to the Appeals Chamber and say: "Please, when are you going to decide this? We need to have it decided." I will try and send a message that the sooner it is decided, the better. But that's about it. It's beyond my --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we certainly asked for an expedited hearing, and I saw Mr. Hocking, the senior legal officer to the Appeals Chamber, the other day and reminded him we didn't want to finish the case before we got the decision from the Appeals Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, and I can understand that, Ms. Korner. And I will -- I haven't had a chance to speak to the President about it, about the need to have this decision, this appeal dealt with and decided.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know whether in fact -- I don't know whether Mr. Ackerman intends to put in a response because that may -- if they know there's not going to be a response.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think there's any need for me to respond. I think the issues are very, very clear. Your decision, it's basically an issue between you and the Prosecutors. I tend to agree with your decision, but for me to say that probably doesn't advance the ball in any direction at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So that's it. Any -- the -- I have got some in fact, I will hand it to you now in case you think you have time to have a look at it. This is a -- again, we don't feel bound or I don't want to send a message that this is a decision that we have already taken. It's being submitted to you for your consideration and ask for, possibly, a feedback, this is the tentative schedule, plan of our work until this case is decided. Please come back to us in the course of this morning with regard to how much time you require for the Prosecution rebuttal and Defence rejoinder because that may gain us a week. And there is an indication on possible suggestion on a site visit which could move downwards. There's no problem there. But it will be then proximate to the filing of the deadline for the filing of the briefs. We have also brought forward the deadline for the filing of the briefs from the 30th of March as it was to the 26th of March. And then -- for both of you. And then give you a further week, that is up to the 2nd of April, to file any possible responses. Have a look at it. And the idea is to have the closing arguments on -- in the week between the 5th and the 9th. If it's not convenient to either of you or both of you, please let us know, and we will make the necessary adjustments. Usher, could you please hand one to Ms. Korner and one to Mr. Ackerman. Thank you. Yes, could we bring the witness in. Usher, could you bring the witness in, escort the witness in, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The witness does not have any protective measures in place?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Good morning to you, Mr. Vracar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to you, too, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Very shortly, you'll start giving your testimony, your evidence, in this ongoing trial against Radoslav Brdjanin. But before you start testifying, our Rules require that you make a solemn declaration, solemn undertaking, that in the course of your testimony you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text of the solemn declaration is going to be handed to you by Madam Usher. Please read it out aloud, and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Please take a seat, and I'll explain to you very short -- very briefly the procedure. You are a witness for the Defence, and that basically means that you will first be questioned by the Defence counsel. In this case, it Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. will be Mr. Cunningham, who you've met already. Mr. Cunningham then will be followed by Ms. Korner, who is the leading counsel for the Prosecution in this case. The fact that you are a witness for the Defence does not entitle you to distinguish or discriminate between the Prosecution and the Defence. Your obligation, your duty, and your responsibility under the oath that you took - you've just taken - is to answer each question that is put to you irrespective of who is putting the question truthfully and as fully as possible. It is our idea to finish with your testimony today so that you can return to your home. This very much depends on the way you answer questions. Please, don't give us information that you are not asked for. Your answers should be brief and to the point. Thank you. Mr. Cunningham will go first.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Your name is Nikola Vracar?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I want to make sure that you speak up loud enough so that the microphones pick up your voice. And it might help you to scoot your chair up a little bit so you get a little closer. I also want you to remember both what I've told you and what His Honour has just told you, that is to keep your answers as concise and precise as possible. I'm going to ask you some background questions. In what municipality were you born?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: The Municipality of Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Were you raised in Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: In 1992, what municipality were you living in?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: The Municipality of Kljuc itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And where within the municipality did you live? A village? Hamlet? What?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: In the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: In the centre of the town of Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Where do you now reside? What municipality?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: I now reside in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And do you have any children?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes, I have three children.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Are you currently a member of any political party?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Have you ever been a member of any political party?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you now about your educational background. Did you attend secondary schools?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And where was that? What municipality?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: In Banja Luka, up until the earthquake in 1969, and then in Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And upon completing your secondary school studies in Kljuc, did you attend university?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And where did you study at?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: I studied in Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And what discipline, what field did you study?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: I graduated from the faculty of electrical engineering.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: When would you have graduated from the faculty? What year?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Upon graduating in 1979, did you put your training in this field to use?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: What sort of work did you do upon graduating from university in 1979?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: I worked in a factory as an electrical engineer to maintain the equipment there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Did you ever go into teaching?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness speak up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I heard your answer. You need to speak up.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Where did you teach?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: I worked in the secondary electrical engineering school in Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Were you teaching there in 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's where I worked since 1983 onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. And sometime in 1991 or in 1992, were you mobilised?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes, I was mobilised, but it was only in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. And what were you mobilised into? Were you mobilised into the military or some other entity?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: I was mobilised into the reserve force of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And the reserve police force where? What city or what municipality?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And do you remember when you were mobilised? What part of 1992?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: It was sometime in April.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. As a reserve police officer, were there limitations placed on what you could do as a police officer? For example, could you act alone?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Tell us briefly how that worked, the relationship between the regular police and the reserve police.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: They were of mixed composition, and the head of the group or patrol was an active-duty policeman. He knew the rules of service, and of course all the other rules and regulations governing the service.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And as a reserve police officer who was mobilised in April of 1992, typically what would your duties be during the work day?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Well, regular police duties. Traffic control, maintaining law and order, that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Who was your direct supervisor?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: He was the chief, Mr. Kondic, Vinko Kondic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Do you know an individual by the name of Dusan Stojakovic?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Was he a police officer as well?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: He was an active-duty police officer, yes, the deputy chief of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Is he a Serb?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And are you a Serb by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. Remember to keep your voice up because that was a little soft, please. I'd like to take you back to 27 May 1992. Were you a police officer that day in Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Were you still a reserve officer on that day?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And did you work that day in your capacity as a reserve police officer?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: That morning, 27 May 1992, did you receive an assignment?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Who is "we" that you just referenced?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Well, it was the patrol made up of three of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. And what was the assignment that you received? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Four of us, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: The assignment was to go to a village near Kljuc. It was called Peci because we had received information to the effect that on the road from Kljuc to Sanski Most, in that area there, barricades had been erected.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: The village that you just mentioned, what ethnicity is that village?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Well, the inhabitants were mostly of mixed ethnicity, Muslims and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: After you received that assignment, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: When we received the assignment, or rather the commander Stojakovic received the assignment from his commander, we got into the car and went on assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: When you say "we," as in "we got into the car" how many people got into the car?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: There were four of us. Two active policemen and two reservist.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Give the names of your other three colleagues for the Court and tell us whether they were regular or a reserve officer.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: The driver was Milos Kecman, he was an active-duty policeman. And Dusan Stojakovic, the deputy commander or deputy chief, he was an active-duty policeman as well. Of the reserve policeman, there was myself, Nikola Vracar, and Milenko Bajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: You told us Mr. Milos Kecman was the driver. Where was Mr. Stojakovic seated?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: He was seated next to the driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Tell us where the two reserve officers, you and the other gentleman were seated?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Bajic was sitting behind the driver on the back seat, and I was sitting to his right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Were you all four of you wearing uniforms identifying yourself as police officers?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes, police uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: What sort of car did you get into or vehicle did you get into?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: A Golf.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: That vehicle, was it identified by its markings or insignia of a police car?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. It had all the signals and the markings of a police car.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Were you and your colleagues armed that day?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: What sort of weapons did you have?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: We had long-barrelled weapons and short ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: By short-barrelled weapons, are you referring to handguns or pistols?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: What time did you -- when you left on this assignment, the four of you in the Golf, approximately what time of day was it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: It was around 10.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. And where did you go to -- where was your destination?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Our destination was the village of Pec.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And that village is how far from your starting point? How long did it take to you get there? How many kilometres is it away?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Well, it's roughly about 15 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Did you actually make it to the village that you set out to, or did something happen on the way?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we didn't arrive at our destination.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. What happened on your way to your destination?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Before -- in front of the village of Pec, there's another village called Krasulje which is where they had set up a barricade, a roadblock. And we had to stop some 50 metres from that barricade. Before we got out of the car, they opened fire at us, from machine-gun fire and from pistols, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Let me stop you right there. The place where you were stopped at, I'd like for you to describe it for the Court. Are we in an urban setting where there's buildings around or is it something else? Could you describe generally speaking what the area around the place where you stopped your car is like.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: It was an asphalt road, the usual kind, fairly straight. And behind a curve, there was a block set up. And that part of the road goes through a forest. There are trees on both sides, on both sides of the road. And when we stopped there, we saw the barricade, so we stopped. We didn't even get out of the car when they opened fire at us from different kinds of weapons. Then --

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Let me stop you right there. Let's take this step by step. Where was the gunfire coming from? What direction?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: From all sides. Actually this was a sort of ambush that we had fallen into.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. When you were a younger man, did you do your compulsory service in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Do you have any experience, knowledge of working with handguns and firearms? While you were in the military, did you have experience with firearms, rifles, other weapons used by the military?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Now, you told us that when the shooting started, they opened fire from different kinds of weapons. Based on your experience, could you tell what sort of weapons were being used?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Well, hunting weapons, semi-automatic and automatic weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. When the gunfire started, where were you at? Were you still seated in the car?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: We were in the car, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: And then we tried to get out.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. What happened to Mr. Milos Kecman?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: He was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Where was he wounded at?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: He was wounded in his left leg, the thigh.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: How serious was his wound?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Fairly serious because it was an entrance/exit wound, and three or four bullets hit him.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: All right. The front-seat passenger, Dusan Stojakovic, what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Well, he was a strongly built man, fat, and he found it difficult to come out of the car. And when he stepped out, he was hit, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And what was the result of the wounds that he received?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: He died shortly afterwards, in a matter of minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Did he pass away at the scene?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: What did the two reserve officers, you and the colleague -- your colleague seated in the back seat, what did you do once the shooting started?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: We got out of the car, too, and engaged in the fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: How long were you shot at? How long did the shooting go on?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Roughly 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. Did you ever see the individuals that were shooting at you, or were they camouflaged?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: They were in the forest, and you couldn't see them because it was May and lots of leaves on the trees.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Did your colleague, your fellow reserve officer, was he wounded or injured in this gunfire?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And where was he wounded at?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: In his arm, hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Could you tell - I understand that they were camouflaged - but do Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. you know how many individuals were involved in this ambush of you and your three other police officer colleagues?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: According to our military information, there were -- it was a company, which means about a hundred people.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. You told us that Mr. Milos Kecman, the driver, was injured, shot in the leg. What happened to him? Could he get away from the scene?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: He crawled out across the road, and about two hours later he managed to make his way to a village where he was taken care of by some of the villagers.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: What happened to you and your fellow reserve officer? You told us that you engaged the people who were ambushing you; you returned fire. What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: They asked that we surrender. However, we used that moment when they weren't paying that much attention to jump to the other side of the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: What were you -- were you -- what were you doing on one side of the road? Were you protected in a ditch or what?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Well, yes, there was a slope just underneath the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: When there was a lull in the action, when they weren't paying that much attention, what did you and your colleague do?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Well, we withdrew, went back through the forest.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. You told us that your fellow reserve officer was wounded in the hand. Did you get injured? Did you get hurt in this process?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And where were you injured and how did it happen?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: When I fell down the slope, there was a rock there, and I dislocated my left shoulder completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: After you managed to get into the forest, what did you and your -- the other reserve officer do?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Well, we were separated for a time, but we knew the general direction we would be taking, so we went back the way we came, but through the forest. And this went on for about an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: What time did the -- roughly speaking, what time did the actual ambush, the actual shooting start, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Around half past 10.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. And was it just on the four individuals that were in the one Golf automobile, or were there other people that were with you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Behind us, there was another combi van.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Who was in that combi van?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Policemen were in the van, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: When you stopped at the blockade, the roadblock, how far away was that other police vehicle to you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: He was behind the curve, so we weren't actually able to see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Was that vehicle ambushed as well and involved in the shootout?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Were those officers injured in this ambush?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: What sort of injuries did they receive?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: One of them was seriously injured. He had wounds through his stomach.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And did he survive the wounds?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: He was captured, but he survived.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when we left off, you and your fellow reserve officer were in the woods, had been separated, but had a common destination. Where were you looking to go?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: We wanted to reach Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And were you injured to such an extent that you needed medical attention?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Well, this is how it was. My legs were fine. The only thing was that my shoulder hurt me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: On your way to Kljuc on foot, did you come across anyone who could provide you medical assistance?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And how did that happen?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Well, when I left the forest and went up on the to road, I happened to see some villagers. When I went up to them, we talked for a while and an ambulance came by.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: The name of the village, do you recall the name of it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Gornji Ramici.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: What ethnicity is that village, if you know?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Well, a mixed population, Muslims and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. And in that village, did you find any medical -- that's when you said an ambulance came by. What happened when the ambulance came by?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: There was a doctor, Dr. Kapetanovic in the ambulance. He stopped, and he examined my shoulder.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Did he take you with him in the ambulance?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And after getting in the ambulance with the doctor -- by the way, what was the ethnicity of the doctor, if you know?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: The doctor was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: How did he treat you while you were under his care?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: He was very proper. He bandaged my shoulder, and we got into the car.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Once you got into the car after being bandaged, did you proceed directly to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: We drove towards Kljuc, and it's about 10 kilometres away. And then we stopped at Pudin Han.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: First of all, what is Pudin Han?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: It's a village near Kljuc. It's about 2 or 3 kilometres away from Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: What ethnicity is this village?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Mostly Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: What happened when the ambulance stopped in the Muslim village of Kljuc -- excuse me, of Pudin Han?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: The doctor got out and went to the cultural centre there. That's a building that's about 40 or 50 metres from the road, and he talked to some people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And could you see people around the cultural centre?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And describe these people that you saw for the Court. First of all, roughly how many people could you see?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Well, there were about 30 people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: All right. Was there anything unusual about either the way that these individuals were dressed or what they were carrying?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Well, most of them were wearing uniforms, and they had weapons, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Describe the uniforms that you saw.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: They were the uniforms of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: In these 30 or so individuals, some clad in uniforms, had weapons. Tell the Court if you can what sort of weapons you remember seeing.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: They had rifles, the classical type of rifle, carbines. Then they had semi-automatic rifles and machine-guns. And they belonged to the JNA stocks.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. How did you feel as someone who had just been ambushed, seeing one of your colleagues die, and two other colleagues wounded when you saw these armed individuals? What were you thinking?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Well, that's when I really became afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Why was that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: I was afraid they would kill me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Obviously, they didn't because you're here. But tell us how long did the doctor stay at the cultural centre that day.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Well, for a very brief space of time. Five minutes perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: What happened after that five-minute meeting with the armed individuals carrying weapons in the Muslim village of Pudin Han? Where Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. did you go from there?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: The doctor got into the car, and we went off to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And where is the hospital located at? Is that actually in the town of Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes, the hospital is in town, in Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And if you can recollect, approximately what time of day would it have been that you arrived at the hospital for treatment on your shoulder?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: It was about 1.00, 1300 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And while you were there receiving treatment for your shoulder, did something unusual happen? Were there other emergencies there in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes. Lots.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. Tell us what you saw at the hospital. Who was being treated? Who had these emergency treatments that you've just described?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Lots of wounded people, young soldiers of the Yugoslav Army who were wounded and had been brought in. And they had been wounded at Pudin Han, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. You got to the hospital at about 1300 hours. When did you start seeing these young, wounded soldiers start arriving at the hospital? Approximately what time was it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Before 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. And were these young men in uniform or in civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: They were regular soldiers who were withdrawing from Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. And I appreciate that answer. But were they in uniform or in civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: They were in uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And how many young soldiers, wounded young soldiers did you see being brought into the hospital that day in Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: There were quite a lot of them. I saw about five or six of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. And do you know the nature and extent of the injuries that these individuals received?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Well, they had received injuries from mortars and from firing weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: It came out translated as "mortars."

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Rocket launchers.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Commonly what is known as a Zolja?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Zolja rocket-launcher type.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Do you know whether any of the injured soldiers passed away as a result of the ambush?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Six soldiers died [Realtime transcript read in error "decide"].

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Now, you were there receiving treatment for your injured shoulder. Was your shoulder --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Was your shoulder injured to such an extent that you could return to work, or did you miss work as a result of the injury?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: I spent about three months on sick leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. I forgot to ask you this question earlier, but what was your understanding with respect to these JNA soldiers that were withdrawing. Were they armed or unarmed?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: They were not armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: After -- you told us you had three months' sick leave. After that three months expired, did you return to your duties as a reserve police officer in Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: No. I went to work at the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. What do you -- where do you currently reside at? What municipality?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And what do you now do in Banja Luka? What is your profession?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: I work as a professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: May I have just a minute, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I have no additional questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Cunningham. Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'm just going to say -- I noticed at the time. It has come out -- I think the man said -- I'm sorry, I think the witness said "six soldiers died," and I think it says "decide." I think we ought to correct that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The question was whether he was aware of any deaths. It's not your fault. You're now going to be cross-examined by Ms. Korner. Ms. Korner, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Vracar, I want to ask you first of all about your training and mobilisation into the reserve police. You were, I told us, mobilised into the reserve police in April of 1992. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Had you been a reserve police officer before that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you attend any training?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: None at all?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No weapons training?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: I served the army --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I understand that. But didn't they give you any extra weapons training?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you given any training in your duties as a reserve police officer?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did they give you training in the sort of matters that you would be dealing with as a reserve police officer? In other words, arrests, that kind of thing?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: We were only taught about the basic laws and regulations and the basic duties to be performed by a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want you to have a look, please, at a document which has got the number -- disclosure number.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's a new document, Your Honour. I don't seem to have it. Would Your Honour forgive me. Your Honour, for the moment, can I put this on the ELMO. I think it has been disclosed in advance, but I'm not sure it's on our list. We're just checking that. But Your Honour, it's a list of -- first of all, can you give that to the witness. And then we'll put the English translation on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. This is -- do you agree, and then we'll have to get the B/C/S because it's obvious what it is. Do you agree that what you're looking there, sir, is a list of active and reserve police members assigned to the SJB Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you -- I need it back for a moment, I'm afraid. Yes, can you identify your name at number 20 on the list of reserve police officers.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Usher, could you now put the B/C/S on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you know why your name has been underlined and with a circle around the 20?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, there's some markings by other names on that list that we can see. First of all, Mr. Milan Tomic, did you know him? Number 77, who was a full-time officer, I think.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you just tell us what job Mr. Tomic held?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Commander of a department.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was he the commander of the Sanica substation?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: I don't know what he did exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Didn't you work out of that station?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. What about Mr. Mladen Todorovic?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Attached to the criminal police.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did he have some kind of command position? In other words, the leader of some kind of a unit?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: As far as I know, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may that, then, be made an exhibit. It's P2721.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, may I ask you, only that page that you -- or the entire document?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I think the entire document. It's only two pages, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Judge, I don't have any objection, but I was going to ask if there's an extra copy if we could have it, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's coming down. I'm sorry, Your Honour. It was left off my list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could I have a look at the document before... Go ahead, Ms. Korner. It is being admitted as Exhibit Number P --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, 2721.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, next, can I ask you to look at another document. Again, Your Honour, we've only translated part of it, because it's quite a lengthy document, but it's headed --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This, I think Your Honours have. It's disclosure 4.223. That's definitely on my list, and we can hand it out to Your Honours. I see Your Honours have it. We have it here for Your Honours. And the Defence, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Again, this is --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, all these documents come from the Kljuc Police Station, I should say.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is the plan of the wartime strength organisation and systemisation. Does your name appear as number 111 on the list?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The -- what does the second column show? It's headed: "Post category, management, key, and other"? Third column, sorry.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then we see your education and secondary school -- it doesn't mention there -- yes, it does further on. Is that your name, Nikola Vracar?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your year of birth, 1952, showing you have a university degree. You were assigned as a conscript. But then it says this: "Assigned to work obligation. Yes or no." In your case, it says "no." That's right, is it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And then finally it gives the address of your apartment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may that, then, be made Exhibit 2722. Your Honour, it's a much -- Your Honour, we've now got copies also of the earlier exhibit, 2721. Your Honour, it's a very lengthy -- the whole document is rather lengthy one showing all the persons, and it may be as well to make that an exhibit at this stage. But we've only translated that page that shows him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, sir, when you were mobilised into the reserve police, what type of unit were you mobilised into?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: The regular police service.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Weren't you, in fact, mobilised into something called a manoeuvring unit?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: We carried out regular police tasks, and there was no need for such a unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Weren't you and other members of the reservists formed into a special unit called, and I'm doing the translation, manoeuvring unit, manevarski --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What do you mean you don't know? Was there such a unit in your police station?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: As far as I know, we didn't call it that. I was a police officer, and the department was divided up into platoons. And we were the third platoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I am asking you whether your unit -- well, no. The first question I'm asking you, was there in your police station something known as a manoeuvring unit, otherwise known as an intervention squad?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And were you a part of that intervention squad?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. So you're saying an intervention squad and not a manoeuvring unit. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Basically, it's the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you tell us what the duties of an intervention squad were, because they were special, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Well, we were attached as reserve policemen to the active-duty policemen from that company.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You tell us what the special duties were of this intervention squad.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Only regular affairs, regular business, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, why were you called an intervention squad?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: During the time which, according to you, you spent in the police force, which was I think -- according to you, it was from the beginning of April until the incident at the end of May. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Are you telling us the truth about that, Mr. Vracar?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: During those two months or so that you spent there, what was the duty of the intervention squad?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Regular patrols and maintaining law and order and assisting the regular police force.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what does "maintaining law and order" mean?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Maintaining, preserving human rights, property.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Wasn't the intervention squad used to deal specifically with potential trouble spots?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Wasn't that one of the reasons why you and your colleagues were sent on the 27th of May to deal with the apparent putting up of barricades?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: The barricades were set up, and we went to see what was going on there with the active police officers.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Listen, please, to the question. The reason that you went to that particular place on that day was because your squad, your intervention squad, was used to go to potential trouble spots, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'm going to object. It's cumulative. She has asked this question before, and he said he didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I don't -- I've been through this before. I'm entitled to re-ask the question because he didn't answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, sir I'm asking you: Isn't it the case that the reason that you went on the 27th of May, you were sent to, in fact, it was supposed to be Peci, was because that was one of the special duties of your squad?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And because you were, as it were, a special squad, you received rather more specialised training, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: No special training because we all served the army a year or two, and there we had infantry training in the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you ever go to Manjaca before the camp was opened, the military training ground, to receive special training as part of this intervention squad?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. That was in February 1992, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You were a reservist before you were mobilised in April 1992, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Why did you tell us that you weren't a few moments ago?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: I thought that you had asked me when I had been mobilised.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, sir. I asked you very clearly whether you had been a reservist before April 1992 when you were mobilised, and you replied "no." You're saying that's because you misunderstood my question.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question. I thought that you had asked me when I was mobilised.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's deal with this special training that you and your fellow reservists received.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I say for these purposes -- well, Your Honour, perhaps we can have the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As you wish, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm referring to P1123.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right. We'll have a 25-minute break. How long do you expect your cross to last?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Until the next break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Vracar. Let's deal with the special training you received in February 1992 in Manjaca. It's right, isn't it, that when you were asked who your direct supervisor was, you said Mr. Kondic? That's Vinko Kondic who was the chief of police. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the reason that you, an ordinary reserve police officer, came directly under his command was because the intervention platoon or manoeuvring unit came directly under him. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Well, he was the chief of the whole of the police force, including that platoon, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. You reported directly to him, or your platoon came directly under his command.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes, like all the other policemen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the training that you received in Manjaca was training in the use of mortars. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Zoljas?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Heavy machine-guns?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Hand-to-hand combat?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In which you excelled, didn't you, because you were a karate expert?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And at that training, there were some Muslim police officers, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: There were units from all the police centres, and of course the composition was mixed, Catholic, Muslim, and Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But the difference was this, wasn't it: That the only persons allowed to use live ammunition were Serb police officers; none of the Muslims or Croats were, were they?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: No, we all worked under the same conditions. We didn't have any divisions in the unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what you were actually getting, and this was the first time, I suggest, this had ever happened, was training from military instructors?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: The training was conducted by instructors from the police force, from the Banja Luka centre actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And also by the military, wasn't it? Military instructors?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: There were several instructors from the army, too, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the effect was that your unit and others from within the CSB Banja Luka jurisdiction were being specifically trained for use in combat, fighting?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: All the units that were there, for example, from Dubica, Prijedor, Nova Banja Luka, they all underwent that training because it was a training centre. And the practice was within the defence system of the SFRY that every year in that same spot, whether it be summer or winter, all territorial units would undergo training, including members of the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I suggest, however, that this was unusual training. It wasn't the sort of training -- I'm sorry, I'll make myself clear. It was not the sort of training that you had received before.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Mostly it was infantry training, except for the combat section.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And it was made absolutely clear to you, wasn't it, when you were fully mobilised in April of 1992 that your unit was going to be used in action against non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Well, that's not what was said. But what was said that we would intervene if there was any major unrest.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, let me move straight away to what you say -- no, I'm sorry, one more thing before that. On the 7th of May, a month or so after you had been fully mobilised, all police officers in Kljuc were made to take an oath of loyalty, weren't they, to the new Serbian Republic?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And at that stage, all Muslim police officers virtually left or were dismissed?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: They were still at work.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Maybe for a little time after that, but by the end of May all of them had gone, hadn't they?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, on the 27th of May, you told us that you and three other people were sent to look at some barricades that had been set up in Peci.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You didn't tell us until much later on - in fact, at the time of the incident - that also present at the incident was also a combi containing police officers.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: I said that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You told us when you were being asked about the incident. Where did they come from?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: They were policemen from our police station.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So it wasn't just the four of you in this one car. There were a number of other police officers. How many all together?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: There were about seven or eight other men.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So there's a total of 12 of you, or thereabouts, going to look at this barricade?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes, 12 or 13. I can't say exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Apart from your police officers from the Kljuc station, were there also military police there?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: No. Just the civilian police force.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were there ever any members of the military police present during the course of what you've described as the ambush?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: You mean in the area? No. Not at that point in time, there was nobody.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And all these police officers, including Mr. Stojakovic were members of the intervention squad?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You were saying that some of them are not?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: What did you say? I'm not quite following you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Which? In the car with you or in the other combi?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: In the car, there were two reserve policemen and two active-duty policemen. In the combi van, there were also several active-duty policemen and several others who were reserve policemen. So it was a mixed patrol.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Were some of the members of a traffic patrol?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: No. Except Kecman.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want you to look, please, at part of an exhibit, which is 1012. And I've marked the relevant part for the witness in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's P1012. Perhaps we can have the English on the ELMO at page 6. I'll give the B/C/S to the witness. That's for the witness, and if you just put page 6 of that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, this is part of a report that was compiled by Mr. Kondic relating to activities of the Kljuc SJB. And it says -- I want you to read to yourself, please, just where I've highlighted paragraph 1, which is headed: "Setting an ambush in the Gornji Ramici sector." Let me know when you've finished reading it.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes, I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, does that say there that the intervention squad of the manoeuvre unit, a traffic patrol, and members of the military police, 14 in all, immediately went to the scene to establish what had occurred?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: The military police held the checkpoint which was at Pudin Han. That's not where it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. This is stating that apart from you, your unit, plus a traffic patrol, members of the military police went to the scene. Now, is that right or isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Well, I really don't know. Perhaps they went later on. But when this event took place, they weren't there. Perhaps they were there afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, according -- just read -- go on to the next part of this. Because according to this report when it describes Mr. Stojakovic being fatally wounded, it says apart from Mr. Stojakovic being fatally wounded, Zeljko Despot, a member of the military police, was also wounded. So, is this wrong?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Well, I really don't know what capacity that Zeljko Despot was in. He wasn't in our car. He was in the second car at a distance of about 2 or 300 metres and which hadn't turned around the curve yet, as I said a moment ago. So I don't know that man and I can't say, nor can I say what capacity he was in there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. What are you saying -- where do you say the military police were? They were holding a checkpoint at Pudin Han?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So they have got nothing to do with this incident?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: No, because it's at a distance of about 4 to 5 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So whoever gave Mr. Kondic this information to write this report, according to you, who was actually there, Mr. Kondic has got wrong information?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: I do apologise, Your Honours. Quite possibly they were there after the event had taken place.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: I don't know that. I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but no, no. This report says that in this ambush, so called, this -- not only was Mr. Stojakovic killed, Mr. Despot, Mr. Kecman, and you've described the injury, were also injured?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But you never saw a member of the military police at the scene at any time whilst you were there?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, you can give that back to the usher for the moment. And I want to examine your description of this incident. You were armed with pistols and automatic rifles. That's right, isn't it, all four of you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The policemen in the combi behind you were all armed with automatic weapons.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And when you arrived at Krasulje, there was a barricade, and you had to stop, you say, 50 metres before the barricade. Why did you have to stop 50 metres away from the barricade?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I wasn't doing the driving. Kecman was the driver, and he stopped the car because he saw the barricade.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to understand your description. The moment the car was stopped, something like a hundred people opened fire on the car. Is that what you're telling the Court?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want you to think very carefully about this, because I don't want you to say something without thinking about it. Are you really telling the Court that there were not less than a hundred people opening fire?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Well, this is how it was. In view of the fact that they were in the forest, and that there was shooting coming from all sides, we had that impression that we were being attacked by that number of people roughly. Now, whether it was actually like that, we couldn't ascertain exactly. We couldn't count them all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So it was a positive fusillade - if you understand that expression - of fire?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Coming from weapons, you told us, that were different kinds, so we're talking about rifles, semi-automatics, are we, pistols?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That went on for half an hour?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
